parole.significato: a suffix used to form instrument nouns
-en: forms verbs indicating getting a property or getting more of it
forms masculine nouns, often referring to sounds
a suffix appended to words to form a verb
suffix appended to words to create a neuter noun, usually an abstract noun denoting a relation, social status, scientif…

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ-. Compare Czech běhat, Polish biegać.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bělъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰēlHs (“white surface or stain”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brъzda, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrusdʰos.

parole.significato: Introduces the first of two (or occasionally more or all) options or possibilities, the second (or last) of which is in…
parole.testo: The conjunction developed from the imperative form buď, from the earlier *budi, inherited from Proto-Slavic *bǫdi (“be!”), which was the imperative form of *bǫdǫ (the future form of *byti (“to be”)), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to be, to grow”).

parole.significato: vessel (tube or canal that carries fluid in an animal or plant)

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děva, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to suck, suckle”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dětę, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to suck, suckle”).
Inherited from Old Slovak driemať, from Proto-Slavic *drěmati, from Proto-Indo-European *drēm-ye-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь, from Proto-Indo-European *dus-dyu- (“bad sky”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъzati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewǵ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *golъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *govędo, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-n̥d- < *gʷṓws. Compare говядо.
From hovädo + -í, from Proto-Slavic *govędo, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-n̥d- < *gʷṓws. Compare говядо.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(j)a̋gnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷn-, the stem of *h₂egʷnós.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(j)ědъ, most likely from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-u-, an extension of Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *esenь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-en-, whence English earn and German Ernte (“harvest”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *junakъ, from *junъ (“young”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-) + *-akъ (masculine nominalizing suffix cognate to Slovak "-ák"). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic юнакъ (junakŭ), Czech jonák (Moravian Czech junák), Polish junak, Bulgarian юна́к (junák).

parole.significato: to place, to lay (to put something or someone in a particular place, usually horizontally)

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotorъjь, *koterъjь, definite of **kotorъ, **koterъ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷóteros.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olkъtь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěto (“summer; year”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁tom. First attested in the 15th century.
Inherited from Old Slovak list, from Proto-Slavic *listъ (“leaf”). First attested in the 15th century.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lamati, iterative of *lomiti (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *lem- (“to break”).

parole.significato: moon, a satellite of a planet

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nogъtь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos; inflected forms from Proto-Slavic *jь, from Proto-Indo-European *éy.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *os(ь)la, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-l-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ, from *pa- + *ǫkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enkos (“hook”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pik- (“pitch”). Cognate with Slovene pekel, Bulgarian пъкъл (păkăl) and Serbo-Croatian па̀као/pàkao. Akin to Latin pix (“pitch, tar”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pěknъ, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to fasten, place”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌲𐍂𐍃 (fagrs). Compare Czech pěkný and Polish piękny.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poľe. First attested in the 12th century.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *porsę (“piglet”), from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos. Cognate to Serbo-Croatian prase, Czech prase, Polish prosię, Slovene prašič, Bulgarian прасе́ (prasé), and Russian поросёнок (porosjónok).

parole.significato: against (expresses opposition, protest, resistance, or defensive action)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *protivъ. First attested in the 15th century.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrstь, originally from Proto-Indo-European *pers- (“rain, dust”).
From Proto-Slavic *podъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds; cognate with Czech půda.
From riad + -iť, riad originally having the meaning of “order” (compare poriadok). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ręditi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to fit, put together”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *õrbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Doublet of rab, a borrowed form.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sěděti (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Akin to Latin sāl (“salt”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *strěla, from Proto-Indo-European *strel-, *strēl-, from *ster- (“line, streak, stripe; jet, spurt; beam”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *stergti, from Proto-Indo-European *sterg- (literally “to cover, to protect”). Cognate with Ancient Greek στέργω (stérgō, “to love”).
Originally “what towers above” (see also strmý; from Proto-Slavic *stromъ, from *strьmъ, probably from Proto-Indo-European *ter-, *ster- (“hard”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *stergti, from Proto-Indo-European *sterg- (literally “to cover, to protect”). Doublet of striezť and striehnuť.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng- (“corner”).

parole.significato: in-, into, inside (prefix used to express movement or direction into the interior of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Slovak v-. Cf. v.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *věděti, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to know”), perfect of *weyd- (“to see, to know”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьsь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“house, village”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olni, from Proto-Indo-European *ol-nei. Cognate with Slovene láni, Czech loni, vloni, Serbo-Croatian lȃni/ла̑ни, Russian лони́ (loní), and Latin ōlim (“once”).

parole.significato: to know (to be acquainted or familiar with)

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫzъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énǵʰus. Cognates include Latin angustus, Sanskrit अंहु (aṃhu).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, from pre-Slavic *h₁ln̥gʷʰ-u-ko, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-. First attested in the 15th century.
Derived from Proto-Slavic *sočivo, probably from *sòkъ (“juice”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷos.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *životъ (compare Old Church Slavonic животъ (životŭ), Russian живот (život), Serbo-Croatian život), probably from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂ (compare Lithuanian gyvatà (“life”)). Related to žiť (“to live”).
